d: A subordinate deity, in some philosophies the creator of the universe
r: Greek dēmiourgós “one who works for the people; a skilled workman”
s: A demiurge or craftsman god takes pre-existing matter and fashions it in light of the eternal Forms.
old_f: A half-human hero, in some legends the founder of a city
A minor spirit, in some folklore the guardian of a spring
A sudden craving, in some religions the work of a demon
ety: From Ancient Greek δημιουργός (dēmiourgós, “one who works for the people; a skilled workman, a handicraftsman”) (whence Latin dēmiūrgus, French démiurge), from δήμιος (dḗmios, “belonging to the people, public”) (from δῆμος (dêmos, “the people”), from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂mos (“people”), from *deh₂- (“to divide”) + Ancient Greek -ιος (-ios), from Proto-Indo-European *-yós (suffix creating an adjective from a noun)) + Ancient Greek -ουργός (-ourgós, “worker”) (from ἔργον (érgon, “labour; task; work”), from Proto-Indo-European *wérǵom (“work”)). No relation with English demi- (as in demigod).

d: A disreputable or clumsy man
r: Arabic jālūt (Egyptian galūt), the name equivalent to Goliath; a doublet of goliath
s: “So if someone does something I do not agree with, I could call him a galoot and it would be okay?”
old_f: A tall leather boot
A hooting owl
A small fishing boat
ety: From Quranic Arabic جالُوت (jālūt, pronounced galūt in Egyptian Arabic), proper name equivalent to English Goliath, giant warrior of the ancient Philistine ethnicity; cf. connotations of derogatory uses of English Philistine. Doublet of goliath.

d: An agricultural laborer in Arab countries
r: Arabic fallāḥ “peasant”, from Classical Syriac; attested since 1743
s: The strange dark One to whom the fellahs bowed.
old_f: A brimless felt hat worn in Arab countries
A sweet pastry made in Arab countries
A wooden sailboat used in Arab countries
ety: Borrowed from Arabic فَلَّاح (fallāḥ, “peasant”), from Classical Syriac ܦܠܚܐ (“worker; peasant”). Attested since 1743.

d: Grant in a condescending manner
r: Vouch + safe, written as two words in Middle English
s: She vouchsafed to me that she regretted ever marrying him.
old_f: Guard in a secure manner
Testify in a court of law
Store in a locked strongbox
ety: From vouch + safe, written as two words in Middle English and early Modern English.

d: An important or influential (and often overbearing) person
r: Coined as a nonce word in the 18th century by the dramatist Samuel Foote
s: Silicon Valley panjandrums spent the 2010s lecturing American workers in dying industries that they needed to “learn to code.”
old_f: A large (and often noisy) brass drum
A wide (and often shallow) cooking pan
A loose (and often colorful) pair of trousers
ety: Coined as a nonce word in the 18th century by British dramatist Samuel Foote.

d: A slight convexity (as of the surface of a road)
r: Old French cambre “bent”, from Latin camur “arched”
s: The track was stony with a grassy camber up the middle.
old_f: A small private room (as in a large house)
A loose woollen cloak (as worn by shepherds)
A soft white cheese (as made in Normandy)
ety: From Old French cambre (“bent”), from Latin camurum, from camur (“arched”).

d: Of noxious stench from atmospheric pollution
r: Latin mephīticus, from mephītis
s: "I could have borne the sight of his crutch," said she, "but the crutch and the nephew together really oppress me like a mephitic vapour."
old_f: Of crumbling stone from long exposure to rain
Of feverish dreams from drinking strong wine
Of icy chill from winds off the sea
ety: From Latin mephīticus, from mephītis; compare French méphitique.

d: Smiling with happiness or optimism
r: Beam + -ish
s: But oh, beamish nephew, beware of the day, If your Snark be a Boojum!
old_f: Shining with a pale glow
Built of heavy timbers
Slightly drunk and unsteady
ety: From beam + -ish.

d: Model of excellence or perfection of a kind; one having no equal
r: Middle French nonpareil “unparalleled”, from non- “not” + pareil “alike”
s: O, such love Could be but recompens'd though you were crown'd The nonpareil of beauty!
old_f: Pair of matching dueling pistols; one having a carved ivory handle
Type of mirror used in carriages; one having a gilded oval frame
Breed of hunting dog used for otters; one having a rough wiry coat
ety: From Late Middle English non-parail (“unparalleled, nonpareil”) [and other forms], from Middle French nonpareille, nonpareil (“unparalleled”) (obsolete), from non- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + pareil (“alike, like, same”). Pareil is derived from Old French pareil, from Late Latin pāriculus (“equal; like; of a number: even”), from Latin pār (“equal; like; of a number: even; suitable”) + -culus (a variant of -ulus (suffix forming diminutives)). Noun sense 4 (size of type standardized at 6-point) is usually taken to derive from the attractive type cut by the brothers Giovanni and Gregorio De Gregori

d: A conceited dandy who is overly impressed by his own accomplishments
r: Middle English cokke’s comb
s: And she nearly started a fight between two young fops in plumed hats and flouncy collars: "Clay-brained coxcomb!"
old_f: A small boat steered by the lead rower in a racing crew
A wooden rake used for gathering hay into rows
A narrow inlet where the tide runs strongly
ety: From Middle English cokke’s comb.

d: An architectural support or base (as for a column or statue)
r: Latin plinthus, from Greek plínthos “brick”
s: The queen placed the vase on the plinth so the cupbearer could fill it with flowers.
old_f: A small flat cake (as for a breakfast or tea)
A thin metal strip (as for a door or window)
A long woven mat (as for a floor or bed)
ety: From French plinthe, from Latin plinthus, from Ancient Greek πλίνθος (plínthos, “brick”).

d: A person who has taught himself
r: Greek autodídaktos, from autós “self” + didáskō “I teach”
s: Leonardo Da Vinci is one of the greatest autodidacts.
old_f: A person who rules with absolute power
A person who writes his own life story
A person who signs his name for fans
ety: From Ancient Greek αὐτοδίδακτος (autodídaktos), from αὐτός (autós, “self”) + διδάσκω (didáskō, “I teach”). By surface analysis, auto- + didact.

d: A comic incident or series of incidents
r: French drôlerie: droll + -ery
s: No drolleries this morning please.
old_f: A slow trickle of saliva from the mouth
A heavy wagon for carrying barrels
A cluster of male bees in a hive
ety: From French drôlerie, from drôle + -erie; equivalent to droll + -ery.

d: The first name of a citizen of ancient Rome
r: Latin praenōmen, from prae- “before” + nōmen “name”
s: Julius Caesar's praenomen was Gaius.
old_f: The formal title of a magistrate of ancient Rome
The family crest of a noble house of ancient Rome
The opening prayer of a religious festival of ancient Rome
ety: From Latin praenōmen, from prae- (“pre-: before”) + nōmen (“name, family name”).

d: An illusory feat; considered magical by naive observers
r: Old French léger de main “light of hand”
s: Just for a moment, absurdly over-estimating poor Zuleika’s skill, he supposed himself a victim of legerdemain.
old_f: A bound account book; kept by merchants and bankers
A heroic deed; recorded in songs and old stories
A legal claim; held by a lord over common land
ety: From Middle English legerdemeyn, lechardemane, from Old French léger de main (literally “light of hand”), a phrase that meant “dexterous, skillful at fooling others (especially through sleights of hand)”, which was however treated as a noun when it was borrowed by late Middle English. The Modern French descendant léger de main of the Old French phrase is archaic but still sometimes found in older literature and simply means “skillful” without any connotation of sleight of hand.

d: Panel forming the lower part of an interior wall when it is finished differently from the rest of the wall
r: Middle Low German wagenschot, perhaps from wagen “wagon” + schot “partition”
s: You found yourself in a wide, low, straggling entry with old-fashioned wainscots, reminding one of the bulwarks of some condemned old craft.
old_f: Cart forming the rear part of a wagon train when it is loaded differently from the rest of the train
Tax forming the main part of a peasant’s debt when it is paid differently from the rest of the rent
Fabric forming the inner part of a coat lining when it is woven differently from the rest of the cloth
ety: From Middle English waynscot, from Middle Low German wagenschot or Middle Dutch waghenscote, assumed to be from wagen (“wagon”) (from Old Saxon wagan) + schot, meaning “partition, crossbar," which is from or related to skiotan (“to shoot”).

d: Not produced by natural forces
r: Latin factītius “artificial”, from faciō “to make, do”; a doublet of fetish
s: Manners are partly factitious, but, mainly, there must be capacity for culture in the blood.
old_f: Not based on any facts
Divided into rival groups
Easily broken into fragments
ety: Borrowed from Latin factītius (“artificial”), alternative form of factīcius, from faciō (“to make, do”). Doublet of fetish.

d: Work of little or no value done merely to look busy
r: Coined by the American scout leader Robert H. Link in 1929
s: Opponents consider this another billion-dollar government boondoggle.
old_f: A loose knot of rope tied merely to keep a sail from flapping
A short song of nonsense sung merely to keep children amused
A lucky gift of money given merely as a mark of favor
ety: Coined by American scout leader Robert H. Link in 1929; alternatively “boon doggle”. Compare woggle of similar sense, which is attested in the same period. In the sense of a “wasteful government program”, popularized in 1935 by The New York Times, in reference to New Deal programs which were claimed to feature people making such braids.

d: A behavioral attribute that is distinctive and peculiar to an individual
r: Early Modern French foible “feeble”; a doublet of feeble
s: Try to look past his foibles and see the friendly fellow underneath.
old_f: A short tale with animals that is meant to teach a moral lesson
A thin sheet of metal that is used to wrap food or line a dish
A thin strip of gilt that is used to decorate the edges of books
ety: 1640–50, from Early Modern French foible (“feeble”) (contemporary French faible). Doublet of feeble.

d: Purchased; not homemade
r: Bought + -en
s: Only I strongly expect Miss Niles drinks boughten tea.
old_f: Bent; not straight
Branched; not single
Borrowed; not owned
ety: From bought + -en (past participle ending of some verbs).

d: At right angles to the center line of a ship
r: Late Middle English athwert: a- “toward” + thwert “crosswise”
s: Above, the stars appeared to move slowly athwart.
old_f: At the highest point of a ship’s mast
In the direction the wind is blowing
At the rear of a ship near the rudder
ety: From Late Middle English athwert, athirt, from a- (prefix meaning ‘in the direction of, toward’) + thwert (“crosswise; (cooking) across the grain”, adverb). Thwert is derived from thwert (“crosswise, transverse; counter, opposing; contrary, obstinate, stubborn”, adjective), borrowed from Old Norse þvert (“across, athwart”), originally the neuter form of þverr (“across, transverse”), from Proto-Germanic *þwerhaz (“cross; adverse”) (altered or influenced by Proto-Germanic *þweraną (“to stir; to swirl; to turn”)), from Proto-Germanic *þerh-, probably from Proto-Indo-European *terkʷ- (“to spin; to

d: Verbal misrepresentation intended to take advantage of you in some way
r: An alteration of Scots sculduddery “adultery, lewdness”, of uncertain origin
s: Power? Shenanigan? Skulduggery? Of course he did.
old_f: Hard physical labor intended to clear a patch of land for farming
Careful digging intended to uncover the bones of ancient creatures
Slow sailing intended to keep a small boat close to the shore
ety: An alteration of Scots sculduddery, sculdudrie (“adultery, unchaste behaviour; obscenity, lewdness”), of long-uncertain origin (probably a euphemism). Relation to skull is speculative at best and likely folk etymology. The American spelling skullduggery is in keeping with terms such as skillful and willful.

d: A song in which a line or phrase is repeated as the refrain
r: Middle French rondelet, diminutive of Old French rondel
s: When holly fathers wont to shrieve, Now gynneth this roundelay.
old_f: A dance in which the couples move in a ring around a pole
A delay in which a ship waits for the turning of the tide
A tower in which a lookout keeps watch over the harbor
ety: From Middle French rondelet, diminutive of Old French rondel (French: rondeau). Ending -lay either from lay (“ballad or sung poem”), or from virelay.

d: A pomade to make the hair manageable and lustrous
r: French brillantine
s: It smelled of soap and burnt paper and wallflower brilliantine.
old_f: A polish to make the silver gleaming and bright
A cordial to make the guests merry and talkative
A lacquer to make the wood glossy and hard
ety: Borrowed from French brillantine.

d: A shackle for the ankles or feet
r: Old English feter; related to foot
s: Passion's too fierce to be in fetters bound.
old_f: A soft white cheese from Greece
A small farm or holding
A strong unpleasant smell
ety: From Middle English feter, from Old English feter, Proto-West Germanic *fetur, from Proto-Germanic *feturaz (“fetter”), from Proto-Indo-European *ped- (“to step, walk; to fall, stumble”). Related to foot. Cognates Cognate with Dutch veter (“cable, chain, hawser; bond, fetter”), Faroese fjøtur (“fetter”), Icelandic fjötur (“fetter”), Swedish fjätter (“fetter, shackle”); also Irish feadh (“extent, length”), feá (“fathom”), Scottish Gaelic feadh (“extent, length; fathom”), Latgalian pāda (“foot”), Latvian pēda (“foot”), Lithuanian pėda (“foot”), Belarusian па́даць (pádacʹ, “to fall”), Bulgarian п

d: Full of or showing high-spirited merriment
r: Old French jocond, from Latin iūcundus “pleasant, agreeable”
s: I was feeling blithe, almost jocund.
old_f: Full of or showing deep piety and devotion
Full of or showing great physical strength
Full of or showing jealousy and envy
ety: From Old French jocond, from Latin iūcundus (“pleasant, agreeable”). Doublet of jucund.

d: A comic verse of irregular measure
r: Probably dog + -rel, akin to Dog Latin; late 14th century
s: As he marched he sang a bit of doggerel in a high and quavering voice.
old_f: A small dog of mixed breed
A persistent and stubborn effort
A rigid set of beliefs
ety: Probably from dog + -rel (“pejorative suffix”), akin to Dog Latin, late 14th c.

d: A long boring tediously detailed account
r: Hebrew məgillá “scroll”
s: A monetary policy maker would probably be okay with the whole “improved credibility” megillah, since it flatters their self-image.
old_f: A large stone used in ancient tombs
A small loudspeaker for crowds
A loud shout of joy at a wedding
ety: From Hebrew מגילה / מְגִלָּה (m'gilá, “scroll”). Doublet of magilla.

d: Rapid simultaneous discharge of firearms
r: French fusillade, from fusiller “shoot”, from fusil “rifle, gun”
s: Our fusillade from the left flank caught them by surprise.
old_f: Rapid melting of metal in a furnace
Slow burning of a long cord fuse
Rapid quarrelling among a crowd
ety: From French fusillade, from fusiller (“shoot with a firearm”), from fusil (“rifle, gun”).

d: An almost pleasurable sensation of fright
r: French frisson
s: I felt a frisson just as they were about to announce the winner in my category.
old_f: A thick woollen fabric with a curly nap
A lively Scottish dance in quick time
A small fried cake of dough
ety: Borrowed from French frisson.

d: Not appropriate in application; defective
r: In- + felicitous
s: "Now, you've got just grounds for shooting me," he said gaily, and instantly regretted his infelicitous remark.
old_f: Not willing to forgive; vengeful
Not protected from infection; contaminated
Not loyal in marriage; unfaithful
ety: From in- + felicitous.

d: Unpleasantly and excessively suave or ingratiating in manner or speech
r: Medieval Latin ūnctuōsus “greasy, oily”, from Latin ūnctum “ointment”
s: General Peckem roused himself after a moment with an unctuous and benignant smile.
old_f: Unpleasantly and excessively greedy in matters of money or property
Lacking any trace of uncertainty or doubt in manner or speech
Unwilling to accept or obey instructions from those in authority
ety: From Late Middle English unctuous [and other forms], borrowed from Medieval Latin ūnctuōsus (“greasy, oily, unctuous”), from Latin ūnctum (“ointment; rich banquet; rich savoury dish”) + -ōsus (suffix meaning ‘full of; overly’ forming adjectives from nouns). Ūnctum is a noun use of the perfect passive participle of unguō (“to anoint; to smear with oil, to grease or oil”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃engʷ- (“to anoint; to smear”). Cognates * Italian untuoso * Old French onctües, unctueus, unctuose (modern French onctueux) * Portuguese unctuoso * Spanish untuoso

d: The 3rd syllable of a word counting back from the end
r: Ante- + penultimate, modeled on Latin antepaenultima (syllaba)
s: The words animal, citizen, comedy, and antepenultimate are stressed on the antepenultimate.
old_f: The 2nd syllable of a word counting forward from the start
The 3rd note of a scale counting up from the root
The 3rd line of a verse counting down from the top
ety: From ante- + penultimate, modelled on Latin antepaenultima/antepēnultima (syllaba) (“last syllable but two in a word”), from the feminine of antepaenultimus/antepēnultimus (“antepenultimate”).

d: Lack of honesty; acts of lying or cheating or stealing
r: Knave + -ery
s: Wine does but draw forth a man's natural qualities; and to make them drink would only be to whet their Knavery.
old_f: Lack of skill; acts of clumsy or careless or wasteful work
Love of the sea; acts of sailing or rowing or swimming
Lack of sense; acts of foolish or reckless or childish play
ety: From knave + -ery.

d: A member of a European military unit formerly composed of heavily armed cavalrymen
r: French dragon “dragon; a kind of cavalry soldier”, from Latin dracō
s: The Protestants in Savoy successfully resist the French dragoons sent to murder them.
old_f: A member of a European religious order formerly devoted to caring for sick pilgrims
A member of a European royal court formerly charged with tasting food before the king
A member of a European guild formerly composed of skilled glassblowers and potters
ety: The noun is borrowed from French dragon (“dragon (mythological creature); type of cavalry soldier, dragoon”) (originally referring to a soldier armed with the firearm of the same name (noun sense 1.1)), ultimately from Latin dracō (“dragon; kind of serpent or snake”), from Ancient Greek δρᾰ́κων (drắkōn, “dragon; serpent”), possibly from δέρκομαι (dérkomai, “to see, see clearly (in the sense of something staring)”), from Proto-Indo-European *derḱ- (“to see”)). Doublet of Draco, Dracon, dracone, and dragon. The verb is either derived: * from the noun; or * from French dragonner (“to force (someo

d: Admit openly and bluntly; make no bones about
r: Old French avouchier, from Latin advocāre; a doublet of advocate and avow
s: If this which he avouches does appear, There is nor flying hence nor tarrying here.
old_f: Lie in wait quietly; prepare to spring an attack
Keep away from carefully; steer clear of all contact
Grumble constantly and bitterly; complain about everything
ety: From Old French avouchier, from Latin advocāre. Doublet of advocate, advoke, and avow.

d: Brilliant and showy technical skill
r: Italian bravura “skill”, from bravo “good, skilful”
s: In a final bravura the ballerina appeared to be floating in water.
old_f: Reckless and boastful courage
Loud and rowdy cheering
Thick and flavorful broth
ety: From Italian bravura (“skill”), from bravo (“good, skilful”). Compare bravado.

d: Destroy completely, as if down to the roots
r: Latin exstirpō “to uproot”, from ex- “out of” + stirps “trunk with its roots”
s: The simple object was to expel the natives, and to extirpate the Catholic religion.
old_f: Speak at length, as if to a crowd of listeners
Breathe out slowly, as if in deep relief
Drive from the country, as if a dangerous criminal
ety: The verb is first attested in 1538, the adjective in 1541; borrowed from Latin exstirpātus perfect passive participle of exstirpō (“to uproot”), from ex- (“out of”) + stirps (“the lower part of the trunk of a tree, including the roots; the stem, stalk”) + -ō (verb-forming suffix) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix)). Doublet of extirp. Common participial usage of the adjective up until Early Modern English.

d: An insufficient quantity or number
r: Latin paucitās “a small number, fewness”, from paucus “few, little”
s: Here is where the paucity of our language is made manifest.
old_f: A brief stop or pause
A small leather pouch
A short unbroken peace
ety: From Middle English paucete, paucite, paucyte, partly from Middle French paucité and partly from its etymon, Latin paucitās (“a small number, fewness, scarcity”), from paucus (“few, little”). Related to few.

d: A metal urn with a spigot at the base; used in Russia to boil water for tea
r: Russian samovár “self-boiler”, from samó “self” + varítʹ “boil”
s: Come on now with the samovar ─ and make haste sorting the letter-bag.
old_f: A woollen cap with flaps over the ears; worn in Russia to keep warm in winter
A wooden doll with smaller dolls inside it; made in Russia as a toy for children
A small boat with a sail of birch bark; used in Russia to fish on frozen lakes
ety: From Russian самова́р (samovár, “self-boiler”); from само́ (samó, “self”) + вари́ть (varítʹ, “boil, cook”).
